title: Effects, Refs, and Browser APIs
summary: Sync components with timers, subscriptions, and browser APIs using effects and refs, skip effects you don't need, and share logic with custom hooks.
intro: So far your components take props and state and return JSX, and nothing else. That's on purpose: rendering has to stay pure. But a real screen also has to reach outside React. It starts timers, listens for key presses, notices when you go offline, puts the cursor in a search box, and opens dialogs. React gives you two tools for this. **Effects** run code after React updates the page, to keep something outside React in step with your component. **Refs** hold on to a DOM element, or a value, without rendering again. This lesson shows when to use each one, the many times an effect is the wrong tool, how to use browser APIs safely, and how to package what you write as custom hooks you can reuse.

steps.title: What effects are for
steps.body:
Rendering has to stay pure: the same props and state give the same JSX, and nothing outside the component changes while React calls it. But some components exist to keep something outside React in step with them. A product page checks the stock every 30 seconds while it's open. A chat keeps a connection to its server. A page puts the number of items in your cart in the browser tab's title. None of that can happen during rendering, since React may call a component many times, or throw a render away before it ever reaches the screen. It goes in an effect.

## An effect syncs with something outside React

An **effect** is code that React runs after it has put your component's changes on the page. Its job is to keep an **external system**, anything React doesn't control, in step with the component: the browser's timers, the window, a network connection, the document's title, or a map or chart drawn by another library. You add one with the `useEffect` hook:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(tick, 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, []);
```

`useEffect` takes two arguments:

- The **setup** function starts the syncing: it starts a timer, opens a connection, or adds a listener.
- The **dependency array** lists the values from your component that the setup reads.

Setup can return a second function, the **cleanup**, which stops what setup started: it clears the timer, closes the connection, or removes the listener. Here, setup starts a timer that calls `tick` every second, and the cleanup stops it.

## When an effect runs

When state changes, React does its work in two steps, which the Re-rendering and Performance lesson covers in depth. First it **renders**: it calls your components to find out what the page should look like. Then it **commits**: it applies the changes to the DOM. Effects run after the commit, and usually after the browser has painted the new frame, so they never hold up what the user sees.

The dependency array decides which commits run the effect:

- `[slug]` runs it after the first commit, and again after any commit where `slug` changed. React compares each value with the one from the last render using `Object.is`, the same check it uses for state.
- `[]` runs it only after the first commit.
- No array at all runs it after every commit, which you'll rarely want.

Every value from the component that setup reads goes in the array: props, state, and anything computed from them. Leave one out, and the effect keeps the value from the render it was made in, the stale snapshot from the State and Events lesson. The linter checks this with its `exhaustive-deps` rule, which the template turns on as a warning and the Starting a New React Project lesson made an error in `.oxlintrc.json`, along with the `set-state-in-effect` and `refs` rules this lesson names. The second example shows what it prints. Don't silence it. When a dependency changes more often than you'd like, change the code so it isn't needed: the part on browser APIs shows how.

## Mount, update, and unmount

```diagram effects-and-refs-lifecycle
Every setup gets exactly one cleanup, run with the values from its own render.
```

In step 1, the component first appears on the page. React **mounts** it: it renders it, commits it, and then runs setup. In step 2, the component renders again with a different `slug`. React runs the cleanup left by the last setup, which still sees the old `slug`, and then runs setup with the new one. In step 3, the component leaves the page, and React **unmounts** it: it takes its elements out of the DOM and runs the last cleanup.

So every setup is paired with one cleanup. A timer you start is always cleared, and a product page you leave stops checking stock. Without a cleanup, each change of `slug` would start another timer, and they'd all keep running after you leave.

## StrictMode runs it twice

The Starting a New React Project lesson showed that StrictMode renders every component twice in development to catch impure code. It does something similar with effects: right after mounting, it runs setup, then cleanup, then setup again. With a correct cleanup, nobody can tell: you stopped and started again. With a missing one, you'll see it at once: two timers, two connections, every message logged twice. This only happens in development, so the bug shows up on your screen and not your users'. Don't work around it with a flag that skips the second run. Fix the cleanup.

## Where the files go

From this lesson on, the examples keep their files the way bigger apps do. Each part of the shop gets its own folder, like `src/features/products/` and `src/features/cart/`, and pieces that many parts share go in `src/components/ui/`, `src/hooks/`, and `src/lib/`. Imports from another folder use the `@/` alias from Starting a New React Project. The Routing and App Structure lesson explains this layout, and why teams use it.

examples.title: Checking stock while a page is open
examples.prompt: `src/features/products/StockWatcher.tsx` checks a product's stock every 30 seconds while it's on screen. The output is the lines it logged in the browser console while the page loaded, then showed Ember Stove instead of Trail Pack 45L, then left the page.
examples.output:
start watching trail-pack-45
stop watching trail-pack-45
start watching trail-pack-45
stop watching trail-pack-45
start watching ember-stove
stop watching ember-stove
examples.explanation:
The first three lines are the mount under StrictMode: setup, the test cleanup, and setup again. Only one timer is left running, because the cleanup cleared the first one.

Showing Ember Stove changed `slug`, so React ran the cleanup for trail-pack-45 and then setup for ember-stove. The cleanup logs the old slug because a cleanup sees the values from its own render, which is exactly what you want: it stops the timer that setup started, using the `id` that setup got back from `setInterval`.

Leaving the page unmounted the component, and the last cleanup stopped the last timer. Take out the `return`, and the same steps leave three timers running after you've left, each still calling `refreshStock`. The Calling APIs From React lesson shows a library that does this kind of polling for you.

examples.title: The linter finds a missing dependency
examples.prompt: The same component with its dependency array changed to `[]`, checked with the project's lint script in the terminal.
examples.explanation: The `x` marks an error, and the arrows point at the problem: setup reads `slug` on line 10, but the array on line 17 doesn't list it. With `[]`, the effect runs once, so showing another product would leave the page watching the first one forever. The fix is the one the help line gives: put `slug` back in the array. Removing the array would also silence the error, but then the effect would restart after every render, so listing the dependency is right here. The last two lines are oxlint's summary, and the time and thread count depend on your computer.

steps.title: You might not need an effect

examples.title: Filtering in an effect: two renders
examples.prompt: A first try at `src/features/products/ProductSearch.tsx`, with five products. The output is what it logged with StrictMode turned off, so each render logs once, while the page loaded and then while you typed the letter o.
examples.output:
render: query "", showing 5
render: query "", showing 5
render: query "o", showing 5
render: query "o", showing 1
examples.explanation:
The page loaded with an empty search and all five products, and rendered twice to do it: once with `visible` as it started, and once more after the effect replaced it with a new array holding the same five.

Typing o shows the real bug. The first render after the key press has the new query, o, but still shows 5 products, because `visible` only changes when the effect runs, and effects run after the commit. That render reached the page. Then the effect set `visible` to the 1 product whose name has an o in it, Ember Stove, and React rendered again. Two renders for one key press, and a frame where the box and the list disagree.

examples.title: Filtering during render: one
examples.prompt: The same component with `visible` worked out as it renders, logged the same way: the page loaded, then you typed o.
examples.output:
render: query "", showing 5
render: query "o", showing 1
examples.explanation: `visible` is now an ordinary variable, computed from `products` and `query` each time the component renders. There's no second piece of state to keep in step, so there's nothing to get out of step: each render shows a list that matches its own query. The log shows one render when the page loads and one per key press, and the very first frame after you type o already shows only Ember Stove. The component is also shorter, and it no longer needs the `useEffect` import.

examples.explanation: oxlint's `set-state-in-effect` rule spotted the pattern: a `setVisible` call straight inside an effect's setup, which always means one more render. Its help line gives the three usual fixes: work the value out during render (what the second example did), set the right value when you first create the state, or set it in the event handler that caused the change. Setting state later, in a timer's callback or after a response arrives, is fine, and the rule leaves that alone. The note says the React Compiler skipped this component, so it also lost the Compiler's speedups until the pattern is fixed.

steps.title: Refs: reaching elements and keeping values
steps.body:
Some things you need can't be said in JSX. Putting the cursor back in a search box, scrolling to the newest review, and measuring a menu's width all need the real DOM element. Other times you need to remember something between renders that the screen never shows, like the id of a timer you started. State is the wrong tool for both: an element isn't something you render, and changing state renders again, which you don't want for a value nobody sees. Refs fill that gap.

## useRef

`useRef(initialValue)` gives you a **ref**: a plain object with one property, `current`, which starts as `initialValue`. React hands back the same object on every render of that component, so whatever you put in `current` is still there next time. You can read and change `current` whenever you like in event handlers and effects, and changing it never makes the component render again.

That's the whole difference from state. State is for what the screen shows, and setting it renders again. A ref is for what it doesn't show, and setting it is silent.

```tsx
const timerId = useRef<number | undefined>(undefined);
```

The part in angle brackets tells TypeScript what `current` may hold: here, a number or nothing yet. The second example keeps a timer's id this way.

## Refs to DOM elements

Pass a ref as the `ref` prop of a JSX element, and React puts the DOM element in `current` when it commits, then sets it back to `null` when the element leaves the page. From then on, your handlers and effects can use the element's own methods, the ones from the web course:

- `focus()` puts the cursor in a field.
- `scrollIntoView({ behavior: "smooth" })` scrolls the page to it.
- `getBoundingClientRect()` measures its size and position.
- `showModal()` opens a `<dialog>`, which the last part of this lesson uses.

You'd also use a ref to hand an element to a library that isn't written in React, like a map, which draws inside the element it's given.

For a ref to an element, start it at `null` and name the element's type: `useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)`. Inside a handler, `inputRef.current?.focus()` uses `?.`, which skips the call when `current` is `null`, in case the element isn't on the page.

## ref is a prop

Your own components can take `ref` as an ordinary prop and pass it on to an element inside them. That's how a `SearchField` component lets the page focus its input, as the first example shows. Older code wraps such components in `forwardRef` to do this. Since React 19 you don't need it, and it's on its way out.

## Ref callbacks

The `ref` prop also takes a function. React calls it with the element after the commit, and since React 19 the function can return a cleanup, which React calls when the element leaves the page:

```tsx
<li
  ref={(item) => {
    if (!item) return;
    observer.observe(item);
    return () => observer.unobserve(item);
  }}
/>
```

Here each list item asks a shared observer to watch it, and stops when it leaves. Ref callbacks are handy like this when you need a ref for each item in a list, since you can't call `useRef` in a loop. TypeScript still says the element may be `null`, because React calls a ref callback with `null` when it returns no cleanup, so the function checks first. React also calls a ref callback again whenever it gets a different function, so keep it short, or move the work into an effect.

## Don't touch refs during render

Read and change `current` only in handlers and effects, never while rendering. Reading it in render makes the output depend on something React doesn't track, so when it changes, nothing renders again and the screen goes stale. Changing it in render is a side effect, and both StrictMode and the React Compiler count on rendering having none. There's also a simpler reason: during the first render, a ref to an element is still `null`, because the element doesn't exist until the commit. The linter checks this with its `refs` rule. The one exception is filling an empty ref the first time, like `if (ref.current === null) ref.current = new Map()`, which gives the same result however many times it runs.

examples.title: Focusing the field after Clear
examples.prompt: `src/components/ui/SearchField.tsx` passes its `ref` prop on to its input. `src/features/products/ProductSearchBar.tsx` uses it, and puts the cursor back in the field when you press Clear.
examples.explanation:
`ComponentProps<"input">` is React's type for every prop an `<input>` takes, `ref` included, so `SearchField` accepts all of them and adds its own `label`. It takes `ref` out of its props like any other prop and puts it on the real input.

In `ProductSearchBar`, `inputRef` starts as `null`. After the first commit, React sets `inputRef.current` to the input element. Pressing Clear empties the query, which renders again, and moves the focus, which doesn't need a render at all. Without the `focus()` call, the focus would stay on the Clear button, and someone using a keyboard would have to press Tab to get back to the field before typing a new search.

examples.title: Remembering a timer without rendering
examples.prompt: `src/features/cart/AddToCartButton.tsx` says Added for two seconds after each click. A quick second click restarts the two seconds.
examples.explanation:
`justAdded` is state, because the button's words depend on it. `timerId` is a ref, because nothing on screen shows it: it only lets the next click cancel the timer the last one started. If it were state, every click would render an extra time for a value nobody sees.

On each click, `clearTimeout` cancels any timer still waiting, so an earlier one can't switch the words back too soon, and the new id goes in `timerId.current`. Calling `clearTimeout` with `undefined` does nothing, so the first click is safe. The effect has only a cleanup, which runs when the button leaves the page. It stops the last timer, so it can't call `setJustAdded` on a component that's gone.

steps.title: Browser APIs in components
steps.body:
Browsers give you much more than the DOM: the keyboard, whether you're online, the user's screen size and color scheme, observers that say when something scrolls into view, and storage. React wraps none of these. Each one is an external system, so each one follows the same pattern: subscribe in setup, unsubscribe in cleanup. Get that right, and a component never leaves a listener behind when it goes away.

## Window listeners and timers

A keyboard shortcut is a listener on the whole window, so it's added in an effect. The first example focuses the search field when you press the / key. Its setup passes `addEventListener` the `signal` option from the web course, and its cleanup calls `abort()` on the controller, which removes every listener added with that signal. That's simpler than `removeEventListener`, which needs the very same function you added, and it works for several listeners at once. Timers follow the same shape: `setTimeout` or `setInterval` in setup, `clearTimeout` or `clearInterval` in cleanup.

## Values that change on their own

Some browser values change without your code doing anything: the connection drops, the window narrows past a breakpoint, another tab writes to storage. You could copy such a value into state and update it from a listener in an effect, but React has a hook made for exactly this, `useSyncExternalStore`:

```tsx
const value = useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot);
```

You give it two functions:

- `subscribe(onChange)` starts listening, calls `onChange` whenever the value might have changed, and returns a function that stops listening.
- `getSnapshot()` returns the value right now.

React subscribes when the component mounts and unsubscribes when it unmounts. When `onChange` is called, React calls `getSnapshot`, and renders again if the value is different. It also makes sure every component sees the same value during one render. Without that, a value that changes in the middle of a render could show two answers on one screen, which is called **tearing**.

`getSnapshot` must return the same value when nothing changed: a string, a number, a boolean, or an object you keep and reuse. If it built a new object on every call, React would think the value changed every time, and render forever. The second example reads `navigator.onLine`, a boolean. When your app renders on a server, a third argument gives the value to use there, since the server has no window.

## Observers

`IntersectionObserver` tells you when an element scrolls into view, and `ResizeObserver` when one changes size. Both need the element, so they take a ref. The third example watches an empty element at the end of a list, and loads more products when it comes into view. That's the usual way to build endless scrolling.

## Reading new props without restarting: useEffectEvent

That third example has a problem to solve. The observer calls `onVisible`, a prop. If `onVisible` were a dependency, the effect would throw the observer away and make a new one whenever the parent passed a new function, which can be on every render. But leave it out, and the observer keeps calling the function from the first render, with whatever values that one saw.

`useEffectEvent`, part of React since 19.2, solves it. It wraps a function so that it always runs the newest version, with the current props and state, and it isn't a dependency, so calling it never restarts the effect:

```tsx sketch
const handleVisible = useEffectEvent(onVisible);

useEffect(() => {
  // ...set up the observer, which calls handleVisible()
}, []);
```

Use it for the part of an effect that reacts to an event, like a scroll or a message, rather than the part that sets things up. Its rules are strict: call the function it returns only from inside effects, never while rendering, and never pass it to another component. The linter checks all three.

examples.title: A keyboard shortcut for search
examples.prompt: `src/features/products/HeaderSearch.tsx` puts the cursor in the header's search field when you press /, unless you're already typing somewhere.
examples.explanation:
The effect has `[]` as its dependencies, since it only uses `inputRef`, and a ref is the same object on every render. So the listener is added once, after the first commit, and removed once, when the header leaves the page. `controller.abort()` removes it, because it was added with `controller.signal`.

`event.target !== document.body` checks where the key was pressed. When nothing has focus, key presses go to the page's body. When you're typing in a field, they go to that field, and the shortcut does nothing, so you can still type a / in a search. `preventDefault()` stops the / from appearing in the field the moment it gets focus.

examples.title: Knowing when you're offline
examples.prompt: `src/hooks/useOnlineStatus.ts` reads the browser's online status, and `src/components/ui/OfflineBanner.tsx` uses it. The output is what the banner logged, with StrictMode off, while the browser went offline and came back.
examples.output:
render: online
render: offline
render: online
examples.explanation:
`subscribe` listens for the window's `online` and `offline` events, and returns a function that stops listening. It sits outside the hook, so it's the same function on every render and React never has to subscribe again. `navigator.onLine` is the snapshot, a boolean the browser keeps up to date.

The banner rendered once when the page loaded, online. When the connection dropped, the browser fired `offline`, React called the snapshot, saw `false`, and rendered the banner again, which now shows its message. Coming back online did the same in reverse. The banner itself has no effect and no state: every component that calls `useOnlineStatus()` gets the same answer, and they all update together.

examples.title: Loading more when the end scrolls into view
examples.prompt: `src/features/products/LoadMoreSentinel.tsx` goes at the end of a list, and calls `onVisible` each time it scrolls into view.
examples.explanation:
The effect runs once, after the first commit, when `ref.current` already holds the empty `div`. It creates one observer, tells it to watch the `div`, and the cleanup disconnects it when the list goes away. The check for a missing node keeps TypeScript happy, since a ref can be `null`.

The observer's callback gets a list of entries, one for each element it watches, and `[entry]` takes the first. `isIntersecting` is true when the element is on screen. Then it calls `handleVisible`, which always runs the newest `onVisible` the parent passed in, so the list can load the right next page even though the observer was made on the first render. `aria-hidden` tells screen readers to skip the empty element.

steps.title: Custom hooks: logic you can reuse

examples.title: Remembering grid or list view
examples.prompt: `src/hooks/useLocalStorage.ts`, a hook that works like `useState` and also saves each new value. A product list would call `useLocalStorage<"grid" | "list">("product-view", "grid")`.
examples.explanation:
`readSaved` returns the saved value, or the fallback when there's nothing saved under that key (`getItem` returns `null`) or when anything throws. It runs once, inside the lazy initial state.

`save` replaces the setter that `useState` gave back. It updates state first, so the screen changes even if storage fails, then writes the new value as JSON, since `localStorage` only stores text. The empty `catch` keeps the value in memory when the write fails.

The hook writes in the setter, not in an effect that watches `value`. Saving happens because you chose a view, which is an event, so it belongs with the event, and nothing runs when the page first loads.

examples.title: Waiting until you stop typing
examples.prompt: `src/hooks/useDebouncedValue.ts` returns a value that only catches up after it has stopped changing for a while. The component logs each search it would run, a stand-in for the request it would send. The output is from loading the page and typing tent, one key every 80 milliseconds.
examples.output:
search for ""
search for ""
search for "tent"
examples.explanation:
Waiting like this is called **debouncing**. Each key press changes `query`, so the hook's effect runs again: the cleanup cancels the timer from the last key press, and setup starts a new one. Only when 300 milliseconds pass with no new key does a timer get to call `setDebounced`, and only then does `debouncedQuery` change.

The first two lines are the page loading: StrictMode ran the logging effect twice on mount, both with the empty search. Then four keys arrived 80 milliseconds apart, each one cancelling the last timer, and one search went out, for "tent". Without the hook, it would have been five: one for the empty box and one for each letter, t, te, ten, and tent. Setting state inside a timer's callback is fine, and the linter allows it.

steps.title: Layout effects, portals, and dialogs
steps.body:
Two kinds of UI need more control than an ordinary effect gives. A tooltip has to be measured and placed before you see it, or it shows up in the wrong spot and jumps. A modal dialog has to sit on top of everything else, keep the keyboard inside it, and give the focus back when it closes. Get these wrong and people see flicker, or get stuck in a dialog they can't leave with the keyboard. ## useLayoutEffect runs before paint Recall from the web course how a frame gets to the screen: JavaScript changes the DOM, then the browser works out styles and layout, and then it paints. `useEffect` usually runs after that paint. `useLayoutEffect` takes the same arguments but runs earlier, right after React's commit and before the browser paints, and the browser waits for it to finish. ```diagram effects-and-refs-timing A layout effect can measure and fix things before the user sees the frame. ``` In step 1, React renders. In step 2, it commits, so the DOM is up to date. In step 3, layout effects run. They can measure the new elements with `getBoundingClientRect()`, and if they set state, React renders and commits again right away, still before step 4, the paint. So the user only ever sees the final position. In step 5, ordinary effects run. The first example uses this for a tooltip that flips below its button when there's no room above. With `useEffect`, the tooltip would paint above for one frame, then jump. The cost is that the browser can't paint until your layout effect is done, so a slow one makes the whole page feel stuck. Use it only to measure and adjust what's about to be shown, and keep everything else in `useEffect`. ## Portals Sometimes an element has to escape its place in the page. A menu inside a card with `overflow: hidden` gets cut off at the card's edge, and a toast has to sit above everything. `createPortal(children, domNode)`, from `react-dom`, renders `children` into a different DOM node, often `document.body`: ```tsx createPortal(
{message}
, document.body); ``` In the DOM, the toast now lives at the end of the body. In the React tree, it stays where you wrote it, so it still reads context from its parents, and its events still bubble up through its React parents. That's because React's events follow the component tree, not the DOM tree. ## The native dialog For a modal, which blocks the rest of the page until you deal with it, use the `` element from the web course. Opened with its `showModal()` method, it does most of the hard work for you: - It goes into the **top layer**, a layer above every other element on the page, so it needs no portal and no `z-index`. - It makes the rest of the page **inert**: nothing outside it can be clicked, focused, or reached with Tab. - Escape closes it, and a `
` inside it closes it when submitted. - It moves the focus to the first thing inside it you can focus. When it closes, the focus goes back to whatever had it before, usually the button that opened it. `showModal()` and `close()` are methods, not attributes, so a component can't open a dialog by rendering a prop. It calls them through a ref, in an effect that keeps the element in step with an `open` prop, which is the second example. Use `autoFocus` on an element inside the dialog when the first focusable one isn't the right place to start, like a form's first field. For a menu or a hint that doesn't block the page, look at the `popover` attribute from the web course, which also uses the top layer and needs no JavaScript to open and close. Every piece of state in this lesson lives inside one component. The next lesson, Sharing State, shares state across the whole app, with context and with Zustand.

examples.title: A tooltip that fits on screen
examples.prompt: `src/components/ui/Tooltip.tsx` starts above its target, and moves below when that would put it past the top of the window. The CSS classes do the actual placing.
examples.explanation: On the first render, `placement` is `"above"`. React commits the tooltip with the `tooltip-above` class, so the browser can measure it, and then the layout effect runs before the paint. `getBoundingClientRect().top` is the tooltip's distance from the top of the window, and a number below zero means part of it would be hidden. The effect sets `placement` to `"below"`, and React renders again at once, before the browser paints. The user only ever sees the tooltip below. With `useEffect` in place of `useLayoutEffect`, the measurement would come after the paint, and the tooltip would show above for a frame and then jump. The linter allows setting state here, because the value comes from measuring an element.

examples.title: A modal dialog with focus handled
examples.prompt: `src/components/ui/Dialog.tsx` wraps the native `<dialog>`. The parent owns whether it's open, and hears about every close through `onClose`. In Chromium, the open-source core of Chrome, the focus went to Close when it opened, and back to the button that opened it after Escape.
examples.explanation:
The effect keeps the element in step with the `open` prop. The checks on `dialog.open` make each call happen only when it changes something. That matters because StrictMode runs the effect twice on mount, and because `showModal()` throws an error on a dialog that's already open without being modal.

Closing can start in three places: the parent setting `open` to `false`, the Escape key, or the Close button, whose `form method="dialog"` closes the dialog with no JavaScript at all. Each one fires the dialog's `close` event, so `onClose` runs and the parent sets `open` to `false`, and the effect then finds the dialog already closed. `useId` makes an id that's unique on the page, so `aria-labelledby` can tell screen readers the dialog's name, its heading.

recap:
- An effect keeps a component in step with something outside React, and runs after the commit.
- List every value an effect reads in its dependencies, and return a cleanup that undoes its setup.
- In development, StrictMode runs setup, cleanup, and setup again to catch a missing cleanup.
- Derive values while rendering, do what the user asked in handlers, and reset state with a key.
- A ref keeps a DOM element or a value across renders without rendering, and is used only in handlers and effects.
- Subscribe to browser APIs in setup and unsubscribe in cleanup, and read changing values with useSyncExternalStore.
- Custom hooks are functions named use-something that share logic between components, not state.
- useLayoutEffect measures before the paint, and the native dialog with showModal handles modals.
